title: Check engine oil level
intro: Once a month or before a trip: check the engine oil level and top it up if needed.

mats.n: Engine oil of the right grade

steps.t: Park on level ground: if the car is tilted, the dipstick reading will be wrong.
Switch the engine off and wait about ten minutes so the oil drains back into the sump.
steps.label: Engine off
steps.w: Manifold, radiator and exhaust stay hot: don't touch them. The fan can start on its own.

steps.t: Open the bonnet, prop it on its stay and find the dipstick: usually a yellow or orange handle.
Pull the dipstick out and wipe it clean with the cloth.
Push it all the way back in, then pull it out again, keeping the tip pointing down.
Read where the oil reaches: it should be between the MIN and MAX marks, ideally near MAX.
steps.q: Is the level between MIN and MAX?
steps.fix: Below MIN: top up with the next steps. Above MAX: avoid long drives and have a mechanic drain the excess.

steps.t: If you need to top up, unscrew the filler cap on top of the engine, the one with the oil can symbol.
Pour in the oil grade from the handbook through the funnel, a little at a time: about [[200 ml]] per go.
Wait a couple of minutes for the oil to run down, then check again with the clean dipstick.
steps.label: Oil settling

steps.t: Stop just below MAX, then screw the cap on firmly and push the dipstick fully home.
steps.q: Is the level near MAX without going over?
steps.fix: Still low: add a little more at a time. Over MAX: have a mechanic take the excess out.

tips: Many newer cars have no dipstick: read the level in the dashboard menu, see the handbook.
If you're adding more than [[1 l]] every thousand kilometres, have a mechanic look at the engine.
Milky, coffee-coloured oil on the dipstick or cap: don't drive, call a mechanic.

title: Check car tyre pressure
intro: Tyres at the right pressure brake better and last longer: checking takes about 15 minutes.

steps.t: Check with cold tyres: car parked for at least two hours, or driven only a short, gentle distance.
Find the values on the sticker in the driver's door frame, inside the fuel flap or in the handbook.
Unscrew the valve cap and put it in your pocket so you don't lose it.
Press the gauge straight and firmly onto the valve: after a short hiss, read the value, for example [[2.2 bar]].
Add air in short bursts and recheck until you reach the value. Too high? Press the valve pin to let some out.
steps.q: Has the tyre reached the value on the sticker?
steps.fix: Keep adding in short bursts. Front and rear can differ: read the right line again.
steps.w: Never go above the maximum pressure printed on the tyre sidewall.

steps.t: Screw the cap back on by hand: it keeps dirt and moisture out.
Do the other three tyres, and the spare if you have one: it often needs a higher pressure.
Compare the readings you took at the start, before adding any air.
steps.q: Had all the tyres lost roughly the same amount?
steps.fix: If one was much lower or goes down again within days, have a tyre shop check it for a puncture.

tips: With a fully loaded car or for long motorway trips, use the full-load values from the table.
If your car has tyre pressure sensors, reset them after inflating: see the handbook.
Check once a month and before long trips: tyres slowly lose air on their own.

title: Fix a bike puncture
intro: Flat tyre? Take the wheel off, find the hole and fix it with a patch or a new inner tube.

steps.t: Shift to the smallest rear cog, open the brake release and take the wheel off: quick-release lever or nuts.
Let all the air out. Hook a lever under the tyre edge onto a spoke, the second [[10 cm]] along, then slide it round.
Pull the inner tube out of the tyre, leaving the valve until last.
Pump a little air into the tube and listen for a hiss. Nothing? Dip it in water: the hole bubbles. Mark it.
Carefully run your fingers inside the tyre and look outside: pull out thorns, glass or bits of wire.
steps.q: Have you found and removed what caused the puncture?
steps.fix: Wipe a cloth round the inside of the tyre: it snags on what you can't see. Hole on the rim side? Check the rim tape.

steps.t: Dry the tube and roughen the area round the hole with sandpaper, a bit bigger than the patch.
Spread a thin layer of glue and wait until it turns matt and no longer looks wet.
steps.label: Glue

steps.t: Stick the patch on and press it hard from the centre outwards for a good minute.
Put a little air in the tube, push the valve through the rim hole and tuck the tube into the tyre.
Push the tyre edge back on with your thumbs, starting at the valve and finishing on the opposite side.
Go round the wheel pushing the tyre sideways: no tube should show under the tyre edge.
steps.q: Is the tube fully inside, with nothing pinched under the edge?
steps.fix: Let the air out, push the valve up into the tyre and work the edge down until no tube shows.

steps.t: Pump to the pressure printed on the tyre sidewall, refit the wheel and close the brake release.
steps.w: Before riding off, make sure the wheel is tight and the brakes really stop you.

tips: Two small parallel holes (a snakebite) come from riding too soft: keep the tyre at the right pressure.
Out on a ride, fit a new tube and patch the punctured one at home in peace.
Cut tyre or tubeless setup: you need a new tyre or a trip to the bike shop.

title: Fit snow chains
intro: When the road turns white: fit chains on the drive wheels in a few minutes, calmly.

mats.n: Snow chains in the right size

steps.t: Do a practice run at home on dry ground and check the chain size matches the size on the tyre sidewall.
Stop somewhere safe off the road: hazard lights on, handbrake on, engine off, hi-vis vest on.
steps.w: Never at the edge of the lane: cars can't stop in time on snow. Find a lay-by or car park.

steps.t: Find the drive wheels: usually the front ones. For rear-wheel drive or 4x4, check the handbook.
Unroll the chain and lay it flat on the ground, with no knots or twisted links.
Drape the chain behind and over the tyre, cable on the inside, and close the cable low down behind the wheel.
Pull the chain over the front of the tyre and hook the outer ends together as high up as you can.
Get in and drive forward slowly about [[1 m]]: the part that was under the tyre comes free.
Hook up the missing section and tighten with the tensioner until the chain hugs the tyre.
Check all the way round: chain centred on the tread, no twisted links, all hooks closed.
steps.q: Is the chain centred, with no twisted links and all hooks closed?
steps.fix: Loosen it, straighten the twisted part and hook up again: it must sit evenly all the way round.

steps.t: Do the other drive wheel the same way.
After [[200-300 m]], stop safely again and retighten: the chain settles and goes slack.
steps.q: Is the chain still tight after a few hundred metres?
steps.fix: Tighten it again at the tensioner. If it keeps loosening, check it's the right size for the tyre.

steps.t: Drive gently, no faster than 50 km/h or the speed on the pack, and take them off once the road is clear.
steps.w: On clear tarmac chains break and damage tyres and road: take them off straight away.

tips: Keep gloves, a torch and a bag to kneel on with the chains: it makes a big difference in the snow.
Some cars only take low-profile chains ([[9 mm]]) or snow socks: check the handbook.
After use, rinse them in lukewarm water and let them dry before packing away, so they don't rust.

title: Adjust bike brakes
intro: Spongy or rubbing brakes? Tune them with the barrel adjuster and realign the pads on the rim.

steps.t: Stand the bike securely, on a stand or upside down, and spin the wheel: the rim should run straight.
Look at the pads: if the grooves are gone or you've reached the wear line, they need replacing.
steps.q: Do the pads still have clearly visible grooves?
steps.fix: No: fit new pads of the same type, suited to your rim (alloy or carbon), before carrying on.

steps.t: Wipe the rim's braking surface and the pads with the cloth, picking out any grit or metal bits.
Spongy brake? Turn the barrel adjuster by the lever out one turn at a time until it bites before halfway.
Adjuster maxed out? Screw it back in, loosen the cable clamp bolt, pull the cable [[2-3 mm]] tighter and retighten.
Loosen the pad bolt, hold the lever squeezed and set the pad flat on the rim, [[1 mm]] below the top edge. Tighten.
steps.q: Does the pad meet the rim fully without touching the tyre?
steps.fix: Loosen the bolt again, keep the lever squeezed and line the pad up with the rim before tightening.

steps.t: If one pad rubs, turn the small spring screw on that arm a quarter turn at a time until both gaps match.
Squeeze the lever hard a few times and spin the wheel: no rubbing, lever clear of the bar, cable not frayed.
Test at walking pace somewhere quiet, one brake at a time, before you ride normally.
steps.w: Stay out of traffic until both brakes stop you firmly at walking pace.

tips: Squealing? Angle the pad so its front touches the rim [[1 mm]] before the back (toe-in).
Frayed or rusty cable: replace it. It's cheap and makes the brake feel light again.
Hydraulic disc brakes (hose, no cable): don't open them, take the bike to a shop.
